title: Trump PAC Spends  Million in Donor Funds on Legal Defense
description_short: Trump PAC Spends  Million in Donor Funds on Legal Defense
description_medium: Federal election records revealed that Donald Trump Save America PAC spent over  million on legal fees in 2023, using donor money raised for political activities to fund his criminal defense. Donors were not informed their contributions would pay Trump attorneys. FEC complaints were filed over the arrangement. Trump various legal entities collectively spent hundreds of millions on lawyers across multiple criminal and civil cases, raising questions about whether his campaign was primarily a legal defense fund.
description_long: The linked BBC report, published September 23, 2022, cites federal election filings showing that Save America PAC paid more than $1.12 million in legal fees during 2022, including over $942,000 to Alina Habba’s firm for work connected to New York Attorney General Letitia James’s fraud case. The article also says another lawyer representing Trump’s adult children received nearly $185,000, and notes that the Republican National Committee had paid some legal bills. It describes a campaign-finance gray area and reports that experts saw no indication the payments violated a statute. This source does not support the title’s missing dollar figure or the supplied medium’s claim about spending in 2023; it covers different dates and does not document the specific FEC complaints described there. The amount, period, recipients, and complaint status for the 2023 allegation require the relevant FEC filing and complaint records before this entry can be completed.

title: Trump Deploys Supporters as 'Poll Watchers' — Voter Intimidation at the Polls
description_short: Trump Deploys Supporters as 'Poll Watchers' — Voter Intimidation at the Polls
description_medium: Reuters documented disruptions during a July 2024 Milwaukee-area primary, where pro-Trump observers challenged absentee ballots and election workers reported delays. Officials said at least nine observers acted in coordination across several Glendale sites and the central count; police were called and two watchers were told to leave. Reuters did not establish Trump campaign direction or verify a separate group's projected deployment total.
description_long: In October 2024, Reuters reported on a July primary in Wisconsin, where activists supporting Donald Trump’s false claims about the 2020 election challenged absentee ballots as workers counted them. Election officials described objections to ordinary procedures, including how names were read and whether ballot envelopes contained a requested form. Officials said the challenges delayed work and were intended to intimidate staff. At least nine observers acted in coordination across three Glendale sites and Milwaukee’s central count, according to officials; the city’s Democratic mayor said police were called and two observers were ordered to leave after their challenges were found baseless. The article also reports the Republican National Committee and state party trained more than 5,000 observers, while a separate activist group projected up to 1,500 deployments—a number Reuters could not independently verify. The account establishes local incidents and planned monitoring, but not that Trump personally directed the observers or that courts issued orders across multiple states. Those broader claims need separate documentation.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Deploys Supporters as 'Poll Watchers' — Voter Intimidation at the Polls
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Deploys Supporters as 'Poll Watchers' — Voter Intimidation at the Polls

notes: Reuters documents the July 2 Milwaukee-area primary disruptions, including at least nine coordinated observers and two watchers ordered to leave. It does not establish Trump campaign direction, other-state incidents, or court orders; it also could not verify one activist group’s projected number.

title: Trump Ends EV Subsidies and Charging Infrastructure Funding
description_short: Trump Ends EV Subsidies and Charging Infrastructure Funding
description_medium: On Jan. 20, 2025, Trump revoked Biden's nonbinding 2030 goal for electric vehicles and paused distribution of unspent money from a $5 billion charging-station program. Reuters reported that the order also asked agencies to consider tax credits and emissions rules. It did not say all EV subsidies had ended immediately or identify specific grants and projects affected.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, Trump revoked a Biden executive order that set a nonbinding goal for half of new vehicle sales to be electric by 2030. Reuters reported that the new order halted distribution of unspent federal funds for charging stations from a $5 billion program, called for ending a state waiver for zero-emission vehicle rules, and asked the administration to consider eliminating EV tax credits. The distinction matters: the report describes a pause on unspent charging funds and a review of tax credits, not the immediate cancellation of every EV subsidy or every project supported by the Inflation Reduction Act. It also describes planned reviews of emissions rules and waivers, rather than completed changes to each one. The article does not list the grants affected, the dollars already obligated or disbursed, or the construction status of individual projects. Those records are needed to determine which communities or charging sites experienced a concrete funding interruption and what became of them.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Ends EV Subsidies and Charging Infrastructure Funding
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Ends EV Subsidies and Charging Infrastructure Funding

notes: Reuters says the order paused unspent funds from a $5 billion charging program and directed agencies to consider ending EV tax credits; it does not show credits were immediately eliminated. It does not identify affected grants, amounts, or project status.

title: Trump FCC Chair Brendan Carr Investigates CBS, ABC, NBC, NPR Licenses
description_short: Trump FCC Chair Brendan Carr Investigates CBS, ABC, NBC, NPR Licenses
description_medium: NPR reported that Trump urged the FCC to revoke ABC and NBC licenses and that Chair Brendan Carr opened formal reviews involving ABC, CBS, NBC, NPR and PBS. Local affiliates, not national networks, hold the broadcast licenses. The report does not provide docket records or the legal grounds for each review, so it does not establish that every outlet faced a license-revocation proceeding.
description_long: In an August 2025 social media post, Trump called for ABC and NBC to lose broadcast licenses over coverage he described as unfair. NPR’s report says FCC Chair Brendan Carr had launched formal reviews of ABC, CBS, NBC, NPR, and PBS, and separate investigations of the parent companies of ABC and NBC concerning diversity policies. The legal distinction is important: national networks do not hold broadcast licenses; local affiliates do. The story places Trump’s demand alongside agency scrutiny but does not establish that the FCC opened proceedings to revoke licenses for all the named outlets. Nor does it identify the docket numbers, specific legal grounds, or procedural status for each review. The source therefore supports describing a presidential demand and a set of regulatory reviews, including CBS and NPR, but not the stronger claim that those networks’ licenses were formally investigated or threatened with revocation. The underlying FCC notices and docket records are needed to identify the proceedings and their legal basis precisely.

preserved_fields.title: Trump FCC Chair Brendan Carr Investigates CBS, ABC, NBC, NPR Licenses
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump FCC Chair Brendan Carr Investigates CBS, ABC, NBC, NPR Licenses

notes: NPR confirms Carr’s reviews included ABC, CBS, NBC, NPR, and PBS and clarifies that affiliates, not national networks, hold broadcast licenses. The linked report does not provide docket records or the legal grounds for each review.

title: Mar-a-Lago Foreign Government Access: Heads of State Hold Summits at Members-Only Club
description_short: Mar-a-Lago Foreign Government Access: Heads of State Hold Summits at Members-Only Club
description_medium: Reuters reported that Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni made an unannounced visit to Mar-a-Lago in January 2025 to meet then-president-elect Trump. Italy's deputy prime minister said they discussed cooperation and detained journalist Cecilia Sala, but no detailed account of the meeting was released. The report does not identify club-member access or any classified information exposed.
description_long: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni made an unannounced visit to Mar-a-Lago in early January 2025 to meet Trump before his inauguration. Reuters reported that she described the visit positively and said she was ready to work with him. The article said no detailed account of the talks was released; Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini said the discussion covered peace, industrial and commercial cooperation, security, and the case of Italian journalist Cecilia Sala, then detained in Iran. This report documents one meeting at Trump’s private Florida residence, not a series of diplomatic summits, and does not describe what club members could hear or see. It provides no evidence that a member accessed classified material or that the meeting exposed classified information. The supplied synopsis’s claims about membership payments and sensitive discussions therefore remain unsupported by the linked account. A fuller attendee list, reliable records of the conversation, and evidence about access to classified material are needed before those claims can be stated.

preserved_fields.title: Mar-a-Lago Foreign Government Access: Heads of State Hold Summits at Members-Only Club
preserved_fields.description_short: Mar-a-Lago Foreign Government Access: Heads of State Hold Summits at Members-Only Club

notes: Reuters documents one unannounced Meloni–Trump meeting at Mar-a-Lago and reports Salvini’s summary of topics; it says no detailed account was released. It does not identify club-member access or any classified information exposed.

title: Trump Says, 'I Understand Money Better Than Anybody'
description_short: Trump Says, 'I Understand Money Better Than Anybody'
description_medium: During the 2016 campaign, Trump said, 'I understand money better than anybody,' while making broader claims about his economic expertise. The stored quotation that he knew more about money than 'anyone that's ever lived' was not verified and should be replaced with the documented wording.
description_long: Donald Trump made the “I understand money better than anybody” remark during a June 21, 2016 interview about how he would finance his general-election campaign. A contemporaneous TODAY report and broadcast transcript place the line in a discussion of fundraising, not a detailed economic-policy proposal. Trump said he had spent $55 million of his own money to win the primaries, said he might do the same in the general election, and complained that Republican officials had been slow to support him. He also said he could win without the party’s help but would welcome it. A Washington Post compilation later quoted the line and expanded it with Trump’s comparison to Hillary Clinton and his claim to be strong on the economy. Read in the original exchange, the boast served as part of his argument about his financial independence and campaign resources. The interview documents what he claimed about his spending and fundraising; it does not independently verify the $55 million figure or establish the accuracy of his wider economic claims.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Says, 'I Understand Money Better Than Anybody'
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Says, 'I Understand Money Better Than Anybody'
preserved_fields.description_medium: During the 2016 campaign, Trump said, 'I understand money better than anybody,' while making broader claims about his economic expertise. notes: The Washington Post links the quote to June 2016; the June 21 TODAY interview/transcript places it in a discussion of campaign self-funding, his reported $55 million primary spend, and RNC support. No separate policy discussion is attached to the remark.

title: Disbands NSC Pandemic Response Unit
description_short: The White House eliminated the National Security Council’s global health security team, weakening pandemic preparedness.
description_medium: The NSC's global health security unit monitored emerging outbreaks, coordinated agencies and supported science-based White House communication. A contemporaneous Los Angeles Times account attributed its disbandment to national security adviser John Bolton and quoted the administration describing a streamlining effort. The full staff roster, reassignment of duties and operational effects are not documented in that report.
description_long: The White House’s National Security Council had a global health security and biodefense unit responsible for watching for emerging outbreaks, coordinating federal agencies, and supporting public communication grounded in science. The linked TIME page no longer serves the article and returns a 404. A contemporaneous Los Angeles Times reprint of reporting on the decision attributes it to then-national security adviser John Bolton and quotes an NSC spokesperson describing the change as an effort to reduce bureaucracy and combine offices with similar missions. That account identifies the unit’s broad responsibilities, but the available text does not provide a complete roster of the staff affected or a detailed map of where each function went after the reorganization. It also does not establish a specific operational consequence immediately after the team was disbanded. Those details matter to distinguish a change in reporting structure from the elimination of particular preparedness functions. The reorganization can be described, but its staffing and operational effects require the original article or administrative records.

preserved_fields.title: Disbands NSC Pandemic Response Unit
preserved_fields.description_short: The White House eliminated the National Security Council’s global health security team, weakening pandemic preparedness.

notes: The linked TIME page returns 404. An accessible LA Times reprint attributes the decision to John Bolton, lists the unit’s three broad duties, and gives the administration’s streamlining rationale. It does not provide the full staff list, where work was reassigned, or documented operational effects.

title: DOJ Appoints Special Counsel Jack Smith
description_short: Attorney General Merrick Garland appointed Jack Smith as special counsel to oversee investigations into Trump.
description_medium: Attorney General Merrick Garland appointed Jack Smith in November 2022 to continue investigations into the 2020 election transfer and classified documents, including possible federal crimes arising from them. The linked DOJ press-release address now returns a 404; an official video transcript confirms the announcement but does not include the written order's detailed oversight and reporting terms.
description_long: Attorney General Merrick Garland announced Jack Smith’s appointment as special counsel on November 18, 2022. The official DOJ statement described two assignments: the investigation into possible unlawful interference with the transfer of power after the 2020 election, including the January 6 certification, and the investigation into classified records removed from the White House and possible obstruction at Mar-a-Lago. Garland said Smith could continue both investigations and prosecute federal crimes arising from them, exercising independent prosecutorial judgment. The linked Justice Department press-release address now returns a 404, though an official DOJ video transcript preserves the announcement. That transcript does not provide the full written appointment order or its detailed oversight and reporting provisions. Those terms govern the special counsel’s relationship with the Attorney General and what is made public, so they should not be inferred from the appointment announcement alone. The order or an accessible official copy is still needed for a complete account of scope and supervision.

preserved_fields.title: DOJ Appoints Special Counsel Jack Smith
preserved_fields.description_short: Attorney General Merrick Garland appointed Jack Smith as special counsel to oversee investigations into Trump.

notes: The linked DOJ URL returns 404. The official DOJ announcement video confirms the two investigations and authority to prosecute federal crimes arising from them, but not the written order’s detailed oversight or reporting terms.

title: Truth Social Scandal: Selling Government Information for Profit
description_short: Truth Social Scandal: Selling Government Information for Profit
description_medium: The Intercept Media and Freedom of the Press Foundation sued in federal court in Manhattan over Truth Social's paid Truth API. Their August 2026 complaint alleges that paying subscribers receive faster access to Trump's official announcements, with subscriptions priced up to $100,000 a month. The plaintiffs say the arrangement violates the First and Fifth Amendments; those claims have not been decided by a court.
description_long: The Intercept Media and Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a complaint on Aug. 12, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, docket 1:26-cv-06867. They sued Donald Trump in his official capacity, White House aides Natalie Harp and Daniel Scavino, the Executive Office of the President and the White House Office. The complaint alleges that official announcements appear on Truth Social before paid Truth API customers receive them at higher speed, while free access is delayed. It says subscriptions cost up to $100,000 a month, or $60,000 with a three-year commitment. The plaintiffs argue that the arrangement gives wealthy subscribers preferential access to public information and violates the First and Fifth Amendments; they seek declaratory and injunctive relief. The court has not made findings on those allegations. The case remained pending when they filed the complaint.

preserved_fields.description_short: Truth Social Scandal: Selling Government Information for Profit

title: The Last Trump Elections
description_short: The outcome of the next election will not change regardless of what Trump says or does. Trump has consistently claimed that the American Left steals elections at his expense.
description_medium: In an August 2026 opinion piece, Ian Bremmer predicts that Democrats are likely to win the House and may win the Senate in November's midterms. He expects Trump to challenge an unfavorable result but argues state-run counting, courts and Republican officials will proceed with certified outcomes. The piece is a forecast, not a verified account of how the election will turn out.
description_long: Ian Bremmer’s August 16, 2026, EL PAÍS opinion piece forecasts how Donald Trump and the parties may respond to that November’s midterm elections. Bremmer expects Democrats to win the House and says the Senate is a closer contest. He predicts that Trump will challenge unfavorable results, including by questioning voting machines and election workers, while state officials conduct the count. The article argues that the president cannot determine election outcomes because administration belongs to the states; it expects courts to reject post-election challenges and Republican officials to proceed with the next political cycle. Bremmer supports his forecast with Trump’s claims about the 2016, 2020, and 2024 elections, his pressure on Republican candidates and congressional leaders, and his current low polling. These are the author’s judgments about a future election, not findings about how the 2026 vote will turn out. The linked piece does not claim that Trump’s statements have no effect on political debate; it predicts that they will not alter the certified outcome.

preserved_fields.title: The Last Trump Elections
preserved_fields.description_short: The outcome of the next election will not change regardless of what Trump says or does. Trump has consistently claimed that the American Left steals elections at his expense.

notes: The complete EL PAÍS opinion piece discusses the November 2026 congressional midterms, forecasts a likely Democratic House win and a closer Senate race, and predicts Trump will challenge an unfavorable result but not change certified outcomes. Its forecast is opinion, not a verified outcome.
